back2basics.text: Critical minerals are essential raw materials used in advanced technologies, clean energy, defence, and electronics. Processing these minerals involves converting ores and concentrates into high-purity compounds suitable for manufacturing. Domestic processing reduces dependence on imports, mitigates supply chain risks, and adds economic value within the country.

2026-11-05-pm-28b6a38476.deck: The Union Cabinet approved a ₹2,814 crore Capex Support Scheme to promote domestic processing of critical minerals lithium and nickel over five years. This scheme aims to reduce import dependence, strengthen supply chain resilience, and support sectors like electric mobility and defence.

mcq.stem:
Consider the following statements about the Capex Support Scheme to Promote Critical Mineral Processing:

2. The maximum capital support is capped at ₹900 crore per lithium beneficiary and ₹500 crore per nickel beneficiary.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mcq.trap: Statement 2 reverses the capital support caps; ₹500 crore is the cap for lithium beneficiaries and ₹900 crore for nickel beneficiaries.

body.label: Scheme approval and duration
body.text: The Union Cabinet approved the scheme on 4 November 2026, with a financial outlay of ₹2,814 crore over five years from FY 2026-27 to FY 2030-31.

body.label: Objective
body.text: The scheme aims to develop domestic processing capabilities for lithium and nickel to add value within India, reduce import dependence, and build resilient supply chains.

body.label: Target minerals and plants
body.text: It targets processing lithium and nickel ores/intermediates into high purity compounds, supporting sectors like electric mobility, battery energy storage, electronics, defence, and speciality steel.

body.label: Financial support
body.text: Capital subsidy of 30% of eligible investment will be provided for setting up four processing plants: two lithium plants (minimum 30 kt capacity each) and two nickel plants (minimum 50 kt capacity each).

body.label: Capital support caps
body.text: Maximum capital support is capped at ₹500 crore per lithium beneficiary and ₹900 crore per nickel beneficiary.

sections.heading: What is the Capex Support Scheme for critical mineral processing?

body.label: Two-stage selection process
body.text: Applicants first undergo technical qualification; only technically qualified applicants proceed to financial bidding where two beneficiaries per mineral are selected based on the lowest capital expenditure support sought.

body.label: Disbursement linked to milestones
body.text: Incentives are disbursed in three tranches linked to project milestones: 25% subsidy after 25% CAPEX spent and 15% equity contributed, 50% subsidy after 50% CAPEX spent and 50% equity contributed, and 100% subsidy upon plant commissioning with full equity.

body.label: Commissioning timeline
body.text: Beneficiaries must commission plants within three years of the Letter of Award, with a maximum of five years allowed; delays beyond three years trigger a tapering mechanism on remaining support.

sections.heading: How are beneficiaries selected and supported?

body.label: Strategic and economic importance
body.text: Processing capacity is vital for national security, economic sovereignty, and achieving decarbonisation targets by supporting clean energy, defence, aerospace, and speciality steel sectors.

body.label: Reducing import dependence
body.text: India currently depends heavily on imports for refined intermediates and high-purity materials due to limited domestic processing infrastructure.

body.label: Supply chain resilience
body.text: Global processing is concentrated in few countries, exposing supply chains to geopolitical risks, price volatility, and export restrictions.

body.label: Investment barriers
body.text: High capital costs, limited technology availability, and raw material access constrain commercial-scale projects without targeted government support.

sections.heading: Why does domestic critical mineral processing matter for India?

body.label: Investment and capacity creation
body.text: The scheme is expected to anchor about ₹10,000 crore investment and create 60 kt lithium and 100 kt nickel processing capacity by 2030.

body.label: Value addition and import substitution
body.text: Processing ores and intermediates domestically will increase value capture within India and reduce the import bill.

body.label: Employment generation
body.text: The scheme will generate direct and indirect employment in critical mineral processing and related manufacturing.

body.label: Governance framework
body.text: A three-tier governance structure includes an Apex Governing Council chaired by the Secretary of Mines, a Techno-Financial Committee for evaluation, and a Project Management Agency for implementation.

sections.heading: What are the expected outcomes and governance of the scheme?

back2basics.text: An election commission is an independent body responsible for conducting and supervising elections to ensure fairness and transparency. After elections, the head of state or a designated authority typically receives official results and consults political parties to identify a leader who can command a majority in the legislature. This leader is then given a fixed period to form a government, failing which new elections may be called.

body.label: Fund structure
body.text: The SRI Fund was created with a ₹10,000 crore commitment from the Government of India, expecting private investors to contribute four times that amount, to provide equity support to MSMEs beyond traditional debt.

body.label: Investment mechanism
body.text: The Mother Fund invests only through 72 empanelled Daughter Funds, which make commercial investment decisions in MSMEs based on viability, growth trajectory, and business plans.

body.label: Impact on MSMEs
body.text: Investee enterprises have grown turnover three to four times within two to three years, with 824 MSMEs supported so far, including 74% micro enterprises.

sections.heading: What is the SRI Fund and its purpose?

body.label: Women entrepreneurship focus
body.text: The workshop targeted women entrepreneurs, noting that 37.6% of registered MSMEs are women-owned, with a goal to increase this to 50%.

body.label: Growth capital importance
body.text: Women-led MSMEs, especially early-stage ones, require smaller investment tickets, investment-readiness programmes, and flexible support due to lack of collateral or long financial histories.

body.label: Linking capital and market access
body.text: Capital support is linked with market access through platforms like Government e-Marketplace (GeM), ONDC, and exports to enhance growth opportunities.

sections.heading: Why does the SRI Fund matter for women-led MSMEs?

body.label: Financial commitments
body.text: ₹8,305 crore commitments have been made against the ₹10,000 crore corpus, leveraging nearly ₹48,000 crore from private venture capital and equity funds.

body.label: Additional funding and schemes
body.text: An extra ₹2,000 crore was allocated to the SRI Fund in the 2026-27 Union Budget for micro enterprises, alongside a new ₹10,000 crore SME Growth Fund for direct investment in small and medium enterprises.

body.label: Credit and equity synergy
body.text: MSME credit outstanding grew from ₹10 lakh crore in 2014 to over ₹40 lakh crore, with non-performing assets falling to about 3.5%, highlighting the need for credit and equity to work together.

sections.heading: How does the government support MSMEs through the SRI Fund?

body.label: Ecosystem partners
body.text: Support is provided through incubation, mentorship, market access, information on government schemes, and compliance assistance by partners like Atal Incubation Centre ALEAP Women Entrepreneurs Hub and Women Entrepreneurship Platform of NITI Aayog.

body.label: Investment readiness
body.text: Daughter Funds advise on investment criteria including market strength, team capability, scalable models, audited financials, governance readiness, and legal structure.

body.label: Entrepreneur guidance
body.text: Entrepreneurs are guided on steps for equity funding such as screening, due diligence, and documentation to improve access to growth capital.

back2basics.concept: Space Debris and Active Debris Removal
back2basics.text: Space debris consists of defunct satellites, spent rocket stages, and fragments orbiting Earth, posing collision risks to operational spacecraft. Active debris removal (ADR) involves technologies to capture and remove such debris to ensure a safer and sustainable space environment. This is important for maintaining the long-term usability of outer space.

2026-11-05-pm-a600741461.deck: India has emerged as a pioneer in active space debris removal with the inauguration of Cosmoserve Space’s Base 1 facility in Hyderabad. This initiative and the announced vision for debris-free space by 2030 highlight India's growing leadership in space technology and its commitment to sustainable space environment.

body.label: Cosmoserve Space facility

back2basics.concept: Renewable Energy Investment and Domestic Manufacturing Policy
back2basics.text: Renewable energy investment involves funding projects that generate energy from sustainable sources like solar, wind, and green hydrogen. Governments often promote domestic manufacturing to reduce reliance on imports and boost local industry, using policies such as the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) which restricts procurement to approved local manufacturers to encourage self-reliance and economic growth.

2026-11-05-pm-e70d62e3b8.deck: India has obtained preliminary commitments of $400 billion from global investors for renewable energy projects, including green hydrogen and energy storage. The government will decide on extending the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) framework within 10-15 days after consulting stakeholders.

mcq.stem:
Consider the following statements about India's renewable energy developments:
1. India has secured $400 billion in preliminary investment commitments across renewable energy sectors.
2. The ALMM framework mandates the use of foreign solar module manufacturers for specified projects.
Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
mcq.trap: Statement 2 is incorrect because the ALMM framework mandates the use of domestically approved solar module manufacturers, not foreign ones.

back2basics.concept: RBI Regulation of Urban Co-operative Banks
back2basics.text: The Reserve Bank of India regulates urban co-operative banks to ensure their financial stability and protect depositors. It has powers under the Banking Regulation Act to issue directions, supersede boards, and appoint administrators when banks face financial irregularities or crises. These measures help maintain trust and sound governance in the banking sector.

2026-11-05-pm-f2e1fa835a.deck: The Reserve Bank of India has extended its regulatory directions on Irinjalakuda Urban Co-operative Bank due to detected irregularities in loan disbursal. This case highlights RBI's role in supervising urban co-operative banks and enforcing financial governance.

structure.intro: Introduce RBI's regulatory framework for urban co-operative banks and its significance.

mcq.stem:
Consider the following statements about RBI's intervention in Irinjalakuda Urban Co-operative Bank:
1. RBI extended its regulatory directive under Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act for three months.
2. RBI appointed the Fraud Identification Committee to investigate the bank's loan disbursal irregularities.
mcq.trap: Statement 2 is incorrect because the Fraud Identification Committee was constituted by the RBI-appointed administrator and advisory committee, not directly by RBI.

body.label: Loan disbursal lapses
body.text: The Fraud Identification Committee found serious operational lapses, including negligence in loan sanctioning, poor pre-sanction appraisal, inadequate post-disbursement monitoring, and failure to verify the end-use of loans.

body.label: Internal control failures
body.text: The committee identified failures in internal control mechanisms and supervision that allowed irregularities in loan accounts.

body.label: Legal notices issued
body.text: Show-cause notices were issued to former administrative committee members and officials, requiring explanations within 21 days, with warnings of legal action for non-compliance.

sections.heading: What irregularities were found in Irinjalakuda Urban Co-operative Bank?

body.label: Supersession and administration
body.text: RBI superseded the bank’s board on July 31, 2025, and appointed an administrator to manage the bank’s affairs.

body.label: Extension of regulatory directions
body.text: RBI extended its directive under Section 35A read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation Act for three more months, from November 10, 2026, to February 10, 2027, to oversee the bank’s operations.

body.label: Ongoing financial concerns
body.text: RBI clarified that the extension does not imply satisfaction with the bank’s financial position, indicating continuing concerns.

sections.heading: How has RBI responded to these irregularities?

body.label: RBI’s supervisory role
body.text: The case exemplifies RBI’s authority to regulate urban co-operative banks, enforce compliance, and protect depositors’ interests.

body.label: Protecting depositors
body.text: More than 7,000 depositors remain uncertain about accessing their savings due to the bank’s financial crisis and RBI’s intervention.

body.label: Importance of internal controls
body.text: The irregularities highlight the need for robust internal controls and monitoring mechanisms in co-operative banks to prevent financial mismanagement.

sections.heading: Why does this matter for financial regulation and governance?
